name: Spider Mites
symptoms: Tiny yellow or white stipple dots covering the upper leaf surface, giving leaves a dusty bronze or silvery appearance. Fine silk webbing visible in leaf axils and on undersides of heavily infested leaves. Leaves yellow, dry out, and drop. Damage worsens in hot, dry, dusty conditions. Mites themselves are just visible as tiny moving dots on leaf undersides.
where_to_look: Undersides of leaves, especially along the midrib. Leaf axils where petiole meets stem. Webbing is easiest to spot by holding the leaf up to light.

season.peak: July–August
season.overwinters: Eggs overwinter in bark crevices and leaf litter

life_cycle: Egg to adult in 5–20 days depending on temperature. Populations explode in heat and drought. One female lays 100–200 eggs. Populations can double every 3–5 days in ideal conditions — act fast.
spreads_by: Wind, physical contact between plants, on clothing and tools, moving infested plants
prevention: Maintain high humidity — mites thrive in dry air
Avoid dusty conditions
Inspect new plants before introducing to collection
Remove plant debris
Water-stressed plants are most vulnerable — keep plants healthy
notes: Hot dry weather is the #1 trigger. Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides kills predatory mites and causes spider mite outbreaks. Rotate control methods — mites develop resistance quickly.

name: Broad Mites
symptoms: New leaves emerge twisted, curled downward and inward, narrow or strap-like. Growing tips appear stunted or distorted. Affected leaves have a bronze, greasy, or lacquered appearance. Older leaves may show bronzing between veins. Unlike spider mites there is no visible webbing — the mites are microscopic and invisible to the naked eye. The damage is caused by toxic saliva injected during feeding which disrupts normal cell development.
where_to_look: Concentrate almost entirely on new growth and growing tips — this is where they feed and reproduce. Check the folded tissue of just-unfurling leaves. A 10x hand lens may reveal them as tiny pale ovals but even then they are difficult to see.

season.peak: Summer — love heat
season.overwinters: Overwinters on host plants in protected growing tips

life_cycle: Egg to adult in 4–7 days in warm conditions. Extremely rapid reproduction. Eggs are laid on leaf surfaces and are oval with a distinctive ridged surface. Males carry female pupae to new growth sites — this is how they spread within a plant.
spreads_by: Physical contact between plants, on hands and tools, on insects (especially whiteflies and thrips which carry mites between plants), on clothing
organic_controls: Peppermint oil spray on off days between treatments
Remove and dispose of heavily affected growing tips
prevention: Inspect new plants closely — especially growing tips — before introducing
Quarantine new plants 2 weeks
Do not share tools between plants without cleaning
Avoid moving infested plants near healthy ones
Maintain plant vigor — stressed plants more vulnerable
notes: Often misdiagnosed as herbicide damage, nutrient deficiency, or virus. The key diagnostic: distorted NEW growth. If existing leaves are fine but new leaves come in twisted and cupped, broad mites are the most likely cause. Treat aggressively — three rounds of Spinosad at 5–7 day intervals minimum.

name: Aphids
latin: Multiple species (Myzus persicae, Aphis spp., etc.)
symptoms: Soft-bodied insects 1–3mm long clustered on new growth, stem tips, and undersides of leaves. Green, black, white, yellow, or pink depending on species. Leaves curl and distort around colonies. Sticky honeydew secretion coats leaves below the colony — this leads to black sooty mold fungus. Heavily infested growing tips may be stunted. Ants farming aphid colonies are often the first sign.
where_to_look: Growing tips and new shoots first. Undersides of leaves. Stem junctions. Look for ants — they farm aphids and will attack predatory insects to protect them.

season.peak: Spring flush of new growth
season.overwinters: Eggs on bark and stems

life_cycle: Reproduce asexually in spring/summer — females give birth to live young without mating. One aphid can produce 80 offspring in a week. Population explosions happen fast. In autumn they produce sexual generation that lays overwintering eggs.
spreads_by: Winged adults fly to new plants. Ants move them. Wind dispersal of winged forms.
biological_controls: Encourage by planting dill, fennel, and yarrow nearby
prevention: Strong healthy plants resist infestation better
Reflective silver mulch disorients winged aphids
Control ant populations — ants protect aphids from predators
Companion plant with nasturtiums as a trap crop
Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer — causes lush growth aphids love
notes: Usually a minor problem when natural predators are present. Overuse of pesticides kills predators and causes aphid explosions. Tolerate low levels — ladybug populations will follow. Ants protecting aphids are often the real obstacle; control ants with sticky barriers on stems.

name: Powdery Mildew
latin: Multiple species (Erysiphe spp., Podosphaera spp., etc.)
symptoms: White or gray powdery coating on the upper surface of leaves, stems, and flower buds. Starts as circular white patches that spread to cover the entire leaf surface. Affected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely. Unlike most fungal diseases, powdery mildew does NOT need wet conditions — it actually thrives in warm days and cool nights with dry leaf surfaces but high air humidity.
where_to_look: Upper leaf surfaces first. New growth. Flower buds. The white coating is usually unmistakable.

season.peak: Late summer — warm days, cool nights
season.overwinters: Spores persist in plant debris and on infected stems

life_cycle: Spreads by airborne spores. Does not need free water on leaves to germinate — unusual for a fungus. Spores germinate best at 60–80°F. A new infection cycle takes 3–7 days. Spreads rapidly in dense plantings with poor air circulation.
spreads_by: Airborne spores — wind-dispersed. Very easy to spread between plants.
organic_controls: Baking soda spray (1 tbsp per quart water + dish soap)
prevention: Good air circulation — most important prevention
Avoid overhead watering
Plant resistant varieties whenever available
Thin overcrowded plantings
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer — lush growth is most susceptible
Morning watering allows leaves to dry
notes: Different species of powdery mildew affect different plants — you cannot spread squash mildew to roses. Resistant varieties are the best long-term solution. Milk spray sounds odd but multiple studies confirm its effectiveness — the proteins on the leaf surface create an inhospitable environment for spore germination.

name: Root Rot
latin: Phytophthora spp., Pythium spp., Fusarium spp., Rhizoctonia spp.
symptoms: Plant wilts despite soil being moist — the opposite of drought wilt. Leaves yellow from the bottom up. Stem base may be soft, brown, or sunken. Roots are brown, soft, and mushy rather than white and firm. In container plants the entire plant may suddenly collapse. Often there is a foul smell from the soil. Damping off in seedlings appears as stems collapsing at soil level.
where_to_look: Gently remove plant from pot and examine roots. Healthy roots are white and firm. Rotted roots are brown, black, soft, and pull apart easily. Check the crown (where stem meets soil) for soft sunken tissue.

season.peak: Year-round — worse in cool wet conditions
season.overwinters: Persists indefinitely in soil and growing medium

life_cycle: Soil-borne pathogens spread through water movement in soil. Overwatering creates anaerobic conditions that kill roots and allow pathogens to establish. Once established, difficult to eliminate without removing all infected material.
spreads_by: Contaminated soil and water. Shared tools. Moving infected plants.
organic_controls: Remove infected roots, cut to healthy tissue
Repot in fresh dry sterile mix
Hydrogen peroxide drench (3% solution) kills pathogens
Allow to dry completely before rewatering
prevention: Never overwater — most important prevention
Always use pots with drainage holes
Use well-draining potting mix
Do not let plants sit in standing water
Allow soil to dry appropriately between waterings
Sterilize pots between uses
Avoid planting in the same spot where rot occurred
notes: Root rot is almost always caused by overwatering, not by the pathogen alone. Pathogens are always present in soil — they only overwhelm healthy roots when oxygen is depleted by waterlogging. The fix is not fungicide; it is drainage and watering discipline. Severely affected plants rarely recover fully.

name: Whitefly
symptom_chips: clouds of white insects when disturbed
symptoms: Tiny white moth-like insects (1–2mm) that fly in clouds when the plant is disturbed. Undersides of leaves covered in white scale-like nymphs and oval white eggs in circular patterns. Leaves yellow, become sticky with honeydew, and develop black sooty mold. Severe infestations cause significant leaf drop and plant decline.
where_to_look: Undersides of leaves — especially middle and lower leaves. Shake the plant gently — adults fly up in a cloud. Look for the oval white nymphs and eggs arranged in arcs on leaf undersides.

season.peak: Summer — worse in warm conditions
season.overwinters: Indoors year-round. Outdoors eggs overwinter in mild climates

life_cycle: Egg to adult in 3–4 weeks. Nymphs go through 4 instars. Adults live 1–2 months. One female lays 200–400 eggs. Year-round pest indoors and in greenhouses.
spreads_by: Adults fly readily. Spread on infested plant material. Very mobile — a single infested plant can spread to an entire collection quickly.
organic_controls: Yellow sticky traps (very effective for adults)
Insecticidal soap on undersides of leaves
Vacuum adults off plants early morning when sluggish
biological_controls: Encarsia formosa (parasitic wasp — highly effective in greenhouses)
prevention: Yellow sticky traps as early warning system
Inspect new plants thoroughly before introducing
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen
Encourage natural predators outdoors
notes: Nymphs are more resistant to sprays than adults — the waxy coating protects them. Multiple spray rounds are essential. In greenhouses, biological control with Encarsia formosa is the most effective long-term solution. Adults are most active mid-morning — time sprays accordingly.

name: Scale
symptoms: Brown, tan, or white waxy bumps firmly attached to stems and leaf undersides — look like part of the plant. Soft scale produces abundant honeydew leading to sooty mold. Armored scale is drier with a harder shell. Heavily infested stems may show yellowing, dieback, and overall decline. Easy to miss — the bumps look like natural bark texture.
where_to_look: Along stems, especially in branch crotches and on the undersides of branches. Undersides of leaves near veins. Check the base of the plant near soil level.

season.peak: Year-round indoors. Spring crawlers outdoors
season.overwinters: Protected under shells on stems

life_cycle: The mobile 'crawler' stage (newly hatched nymphs) is the only stage that moves — this is when chemical control is most effective. Crawlers settle, insert mouthparts, and secrete their protective covering. Adults are sessile (non-moving).
spreads_by: Crawlers walk or are blown to new plants. Moved on infested plant material.
organic_controls: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton swab — directly kills scale on contact (most effective)
conventional_controls: Imidacloprid (systemic — absorbed through roots, kills feeding scale)
prevention: Inspect new plants thoroughly
Maintain plant vigor — stressed plants more susceptible
Avoid overfertilizing with nitrogen
Good air circulation
notes: The protective shell makes scale resistant to most sprays — the alcohol swab method works because it dissolves the waxy covering directly. Systemic insecticides are often the most reliable for severe infestations. Check plants monthly in winter when growth is slow — scale populations build unnoticed.

name: Mealybugs
symptoms: White cottony or waxy masses at leaf joints, stem crevices, and on roots. The insects themselves are soft, oval, pink-bodied, covered in white mealy wax. Sticky honeydew coats leaves and leads to sooty mold. Plants yellow and weaken. Root mealybugs cause yellowing and wilting with no obvious above-ground pest visible — check roots when repotting.
where_to_look: Leaf axils (where leaves meet stems) — their favorite hiding spot. Stem crevices. On roots (root mealybugs appear as white cottony masses around roots when unpotted). Under leaves.

season.peak: Year-round indoors
season.overwinters: Year-round on houseplants

life_cycle: Females lay 300–600 eggs in cottony egg sacs. Crawlers emerge and move to feeding sites. Life cycle 6–10 weeks. Several overlapping generations per year — control requires persistent effort.
spreads_by: Crawlers walk between touching plants. On hands, tools, clothing. New infested plants.
organic_controls: 70% isopropyl alcohol on cotton swab — most effective direct treatment
Neem oil drench for root mealybugs
prevention: Inspect all new plants before introducing
Quarantine new plants 2 weeks
Check leaf axils monthly
Avoid overcrowding — spreads by contact
Reduce nitrogen fertilizer — lush growth is preferred
notes: Mealybugs hide extremely well in leaf axils and root zone. Treatment must be thorough and repeated — one missed individual can restart the infestation. Root mealybugs are often discovered only when repotting; treat with a systemic insecticide or hydrogen peroxide drench.

name: Fungus Gnats
symptoms: Small dark flies (2–3mm) hovering around the soil surface and flying up when the plant is disturbed. The flies themselves cause little damage — it is the larvae in the soil that damage roots. Seedlings are most vulnerable — larvae sever roots and cause damping off. In established plants, root damage leads to nutrient deficiency symptoms: yellowing, slow growth, wilting. Larvae are tiny white maggots with black heads in the top inch of soil.
where_to_look: Adults hover near soil and fly when disturbed. Place a yellow sticky trap at soil level — catches adults and confirms infestation. To find larvae, slice a raw potato and place flesh-side down on the soil surface — larvae will be found on it after 24 hours.

season.peak: Year-round indoors — worse in autumn/winter when overwatering increases
season.overwinters: Year-round in warm indoor conditions

life_cycle: Egg to adult in 3–4 weeks. Adults live 1 week. Female lays 100–200 eggs in moist soil. The problem is almost always caused by consistently wet soil — dry soil breaks the cycle.
spreads_by: Adults fly freely between plants. Infested soil or growing medium.
organic_controls: Allow soil to dry out thoroughly between waterings — most effective
Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (BTi) soil drench — kills larvae
Potato slice trap to monitor larvae
Hydrogen peroxide drench (1 part 3% H2O2 to 4 parts water)
prevention: Do not overwater — the most important prevention
Use well-draining potting mix
Add a layer of sand or grit to top inch of soil
Do not leave standing water in saucers
Use sterile potting mix
notes: Letting the soil dry out is the single most effective control — fungus gnat larvae cannot survive in dry soil. The flies are annoying but the real damage is from larvae. BTi (sold as Gnatrol or Mosquito Bits soaked in water) is highly effective and safe for plants, people, and pets.

name: Thrips
symptoms: Silver or bronze streaking and stippling on leaves — caused by the thrips rasping the leaf surface and drinking the cell contents. Tiny black dots of frass (excrement) on leaves. Flowers are deformed, scarred, or fail to open properly. Heavily infested growing tips may be stunted and distorted. Thrips themselves are barely visible — slender, 1–2mm, pale yellow to dark brown. Shake a flower over white paper to dislodge them for identification.
where_to_look: Inside flowers — thrips love to feed in flowers where they are protected. Growing tips and young leaves. Undersides of leaves. Shake flowers or leaves over white paper to dislodge and see the insects.

season.peak: Late spring through summer
season.overwinters: In plant debris, soil, and on weeds

life_cycle: Egg to adult in 2–3 weeks. Eggs inserted into plant tissue. Larvae drop to soil to pupate. Adults fly readily. Multiple overlapping generations. Vectors of Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus and Impatiens Necrotic Spot Virus.
spreads_by: Flying adults. Movement on infested plant material. Wind.
organic_controls: Blue or yellow sticky traps (blue is more effective for flower thrips)
prevention: Blue sticky traps as early warning system
Remove plant debris where they overwinter
Inspect flowers of new plants before purchasing
Reflective mulch disorients adults
notes: Thrips are difficult to control because the pupal stage in soil is not affected by foliar sprays. A combined approach — foliar spinosad AND beneficial nematodes in the soil — addresses both stages. Thrips can transmit serious viruses so early control is important.

name: Japanese Beetle
symptoms: Leaves skeletonized — only the veins remain after beetles consume the leaf tissue between them, giving a lacy appearance. Flowers eaten. Metallic green and copper beetles 1cm long feed in groups. The larval stage (white C-shaped grubs) lives in soil and damages grass roots causing brown patches in lawns.
where_to_look: Adults feed in groups on the upper surface of leaves and in flowers — look for clusters of beetles. Peak activity is midday in warm sunny weather. Check roses, basil, beans, and grapes first — favorite targets.

season.peak: June–August
season.overwinters: Grubs overwinter 4–6 inches deep in soil

life_cycle: Adults emerge in late June. Females lay eggs in lawns. Grubs feed on grass roots through autumn. Overwinter deep. Pupate in spring. One generation per year.
spreads_by: Adults fly up to 5 miles. Grubs spread when infested turf is moved.
organic_controls: Hand-pick into soapy water early morning (most effective)
biological_controls: Bacillus thuringiensis galleriae (Btg) — kills adults and larvae
Beneficial nematodes (Heterorhabditis bacteriophora) for grub control
prevention: Pheromone traps attract MORE beetles — use far from garden or not at all
Plant resistant species
Treat lawn for grubs in late summer
Hand-pick consistently — reduces population in small gardens
notes: Pheromone traps are widely sold but research shows they attract more beetles to your area than they catch — place them far from valuable plants or skip them entirely. Early morning hand-picking is the most reliable small-garden strategy. The grub damage to lawns can be extensive.

name: Flea Beetles
symptoms: Numerous tiny round holes (1–3mm) punched through leaves in a 'shothole' pattern — looks like the leaf was hit with a tiny shotgun. Seedlings and young transplants are most vulnerable — damage at this stage can kill the plant. Small shiny black, bronze, or striped beetles (2–3mm) jump like fleas when disturbed. Adults feed on leaves; larvae feed on roots.
where_to_look: Leaf surfaces — the holes are very distinctive. The beetles themselves jump immediately when disturbed, making them hard to see directly. Check early morning when cooler and slower.

season.peak: Spring on emerging seedlings, second generation in late summer
season.overwinters: Adults overwinter in leaf litter and soil

life_cycle: Adults overwinter, emerge in spring to feed. Eggs laid in soil near host plants. Larvae feed on roots for several weeks. Pupate in soil. New adults emerge mid-summer. Two generations per year in warm climates.
spreads_by: Adults jump and fly readily. Spread from surrounding garden areas.
organic_controls: Row covers over transplants — most effective prevention
Delay transplanting until plants are larger
biological_controls: Beneficial nematodes for larval stage in soil
prevention: Row covers immediately after transplanting
Delay planting until seedlings are larger
Remove plant debris where adults overwinter
Trap cropping with radishes — they prefer radish, which can then be removed
notes: Flea beetles rarely kill established plants — focus protection on seedlings and transplants. Row covers for the first 2–3 weeks after transplanting give plants time to outgrow vulnerability. Radish is an excellent trap crop — plant near affected plants, then remove the radish when covered in beetles.

name: Tomato Hornworm
symptoms: Entire branches stripped of leaves seemingly overnight. Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches long) perfectly camouflaged against stems. Dark horn on the tail end. Dark green frass (droppings) the size of small peas on leaves and soil below. Partially eaten fruit with large irregular cavities.
where_to_look: Look for the large dark green frass pellets on leaves and ground — they give away the caterpillar's location before you can see it. Trace upward from the frass to find the caterpillar. Check at night with a UV black light — hornworms glow bright green.

season.peak: July–August
season.overwinters: Pupae overwinter 3–4 inches deep in soil

life_cycle: Adults are large sphinx moths (hummingbird moths) that lay single eggs on leaf undersides. Caterpillars feed for 4–6 weeks, drop to soil to pupate. One generation per year in north, two in south.
spreads_by: Adult moths fly long distances to lay eggs.
organic_controls: Hand-pick (most effective) — wear gloves, caterpillars are harmless but large
BT (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray — kills caterpillars within days
biological_controls: Parasitic wasps (Cotesia congregata) — if you see white rice-like cocoons on the caterpillar, leave it. The wasps are pupating inside and will kill it AND provide more beneficial wasps
prevention: Till soil in fall/spring to expose pupae
Attract parasitic wasps with dill, fennel, and yarrow
Plant dill nearby as a trap crop for egg-laying moths
notes: If you find a hornworm covered in white oval protrusions that look like rice grains, these are the cocoons of parasitic braconid wasps. Leave the caterpillar — the wasps will emerge, kill it, and become free pest control in your garden. Never kill a parasitized hornworm.

name: Squash Vine Borer
symptoms: Healthy plant suddenly wilts and collapses as if drought-stressed — but soil is moist. Sawdust-like frass (often mixed with green liquid) piled at the base of the stem, often at multiple entry points. Larvae bore through the stem, cutting off water and nutrient flow. Splitting the stem reveals creamy white larvae inside.
where_to_look: Base of the plant where the vine meets the soil — look for the sawdust-like frass. Entry holes in the stem, usually 1–3 inches from the ground. The adult is a striking red and black moth that resembles a wasp — look for it laying single red-brown eggs on stems in early summer.

season.peak: Late June through July when adults lay eggs
season.overwinters: Pupae overwinter in soil

life_cycle: One generation per year (sometimes two in the South). Adults lay flat red-brown eggs individually on stems. Larvae bore in and feed for 4–6 weeks. Drop to soil to overwinter. Timing is critical — protect stems before eggs hatch.
spreads_by: Adult moths fly from surrounding areas.
organic_controls: Row covers until flowering (then remove for pollination)
Wrap stems in aluminum foil — prevents egg-laying
Inject BT into the stem with a syringe at first sign of frass
Surgical removal — slit the stem, remove larvae, mound soil over the cut
Succession planting — plant a second crop in late June after adult flight
conventional_controls: Permethrin spray on stems from egg-laying time through July
prevention: Row covers are the most effective prevention
Wrap the stem base with aluminum foil or pantyhose
Plant resistant varieties (butternut squash is much less susceptible than zucchini)
Mound soil over vine nodes to encourage new roots above the damage
notes: Once borers are inside the stem, they are extremely difficult to control. Prevention is everything. Butternut squash has harder stems and is much more resistant than zucchini, acorn, or yellow squash. If a plant collapses, immediately mound soil over the stems at several points — the vine will root above the damage and may survive.

name: Cutworms
symptoms: Seedlings and young transplants are cut off cleanly at or just below soil level overnight — looks like a tiny chainsaw was used. The plant lies beside a cleanly severed stem. Fat grey, brown, or black caterpillars (2–4cm) curl into a C-shape when disturbed. Found in the top 2–3 inches of soil near the damaged plant during the day.
where_to_look: Dig in the soil within a few inches of the severed plant — cutworms hide just below the soil surface near their feeding site during daylight hours. Check at night with a flashlight.

season.peak: Early spring when transplants go in
season.overwinters: Larvae and pupae overwinter in soil

life_cycle: Adults are dull brown moths that lay eggs on soil or plant debris in late summer. Larvae overwinter in soil, resume feeding in spring. Most damage occurs in spring when seedlings are planted.
spreads_by: Adult moths fly widely to lay eggs. Present wherever there is soil.
organic_controls: Cardboard or plastic collar around stem (push 2 inches into soil, 2 above) — most effective
BT spray on soil surface in evening
prevention: Protective collars on all transplants
Till soil in fall to expose overwintering larvae to birds and frost
Remove plant debris in autumn
Delay transplanting until plants are larger and stems are tougher
notes: The stem collar is the most reliable and practical protection. A toilet paper tube cut in half and pushed around the transplant stem makes an excellent free collar. The damage is always worst on newly transplanted seedlings — established plants with tough stems are rarely targeted.

name: Slugs and Snails
latin: Deroceras spp., Arion spp., Helix spp.
symptoms: Irregular ragged holes in leaves — especially at leaf margins. Distinctive silvery slime trails on leaves and soil. Seedlings may disappear entirely overnight. Damage is worst at soil level and on lower leaves. Strawberries and other low fruit show pitting and slime. No insects visible during the day — slugs feed at night and hide under debris, boards, and soil during daylight.
where_to_look: Check at night with a flashlight — this is when they are active. During the day lift boards, stones, and pots, and check under plant debris and thick mulch. Slime trails are visible on soil surface in the morning.

season.peak: Cool moist conditions — spring and fall
season.overwinters: Eggs overwinter in soil. Adults overwinter under debris in mild climates

life_cycle: Lay round white eggs in clusters under debris and in soil. Eggs hatch in 3–6 weeks. Young slugs reach maturity in 3–6 months. Most active in cool wet conditions — populations crash in heat and drought.
spreads_by: Move on their own slowly. Can be moved in soil and plant material.
organic_controls: Iron phosphate bait (Sluggo) — safe for pets, wildlife, and soil
Beer traps — bury a container of cheap beer to soil level, slugs drown in it
Diatomaceous earth around plants (loses effectiveness when wet)
conventional_controls: Metaldehyde bait (toxic to pets and wildlife — use with caution)
biological_controls: Toads and frogs — encourage by providing water features
prevention: Avoid heavy mulching near susceptible plants
Water in the morning rather than evening
Remove boards and debris near garden
Create rough surfaces around plants — slugs dislike crossing them
Reduce hiding places
notes: Iron phosphate bait (Sluggo) is the best overall control — effective, safe for pets and wildlife, and breaks down into soil nutrients. Beer traps work well but require daily maintenance. Diatomaceous earth works only when dry. Encourage natural predators like toads by providing water features near the garden.

name: Blossom End Rot
symptom_chips: dark sunken spot on fruit bottom
symptoms: Dark brown or black sunken leathery patch on the blossom end (bottom) of fruit — tomatoes, peppers, squash, and melons most commonly. The patch starts small and water-soaked, then enlarges and turns dark and leathery. The rest of the fruit may be completely normal and edible if the patch is small. NOT caused by a pathogen — this is a physiological disorder.
where_to_look: The blossom end of fruit — the end opposite the stem. Appears when fruit is 1/3 to 1/2 size. Check lower fruit first.

season.peak: Early summer fruit set during drought or temperature swings
season.overwinters: N/A — not an organism

life_cycle: N/A — this is a calcium uptake failure, not an organism with a life cycle.
spreads_by: Does not spread — it is a physiological disorder caused by inconsistent watering and calcium uptake failure.
organic_controls: Consistent even watering — the primary fix
Calcium foliar spray (calcium chloride) as a short-term fix
Crushed eggshells or lime worked into soil (long-term calcium source)
conventional_controls: Calcium chloride spray on fruit and foliage
prevention: Consistent watering schedule — the most important prevention
Deep mulching to prevent moisture fluctuation
Avoid overuse of high-nitrogen and high-potassium fertilizers — compete with calcium uptake
Do not damage roots by cultivating near plants
Maintain soil pH 6.2–6.8 for best calcium availability
notes: This is the most misunderstood garden problem. People reach for calcium sprays when the real issue is inconsistent watering — irregular wet-dry cycles prevent calcium uptake regardless of how much calcium is in the soil. Fix the watering first. The affected fruit are safe to eat — simply cut away the affected portion.

name: Iron Chlorosis
symptoms: Leaves turn yellow while the veins remain distinctly green — called interveinal chlorosis. Appears on young new growth first (unlike nitrogen deficiency which starts on old lower leaves). Severe cases: leaves turn almost white with only a fine green network of veins visible. Most common on acid-loving plants (azalea, blueberry, gardenia, rhododendron) grown in alkaline soil.
where_to_look: Young new growth at the growing tips — the newest leaves show symptoms first. Hold a leaf up to light to see the contrast between yellow tissue and green veins clearly.

season.peak: Spring and summer when growth is fastest and iron demand is highest
season.overwinters: N/A

life_cycle: N/A — this is a nutrient deficiency, not an organism.
spreads_by: Does not spread — each plant responds to its own soil conditions.
organic_controls: Chelated iron foliar spray — fastest fix (absorbed directly through leaves)
Coffee grounds or acidic mulch (pine bark) long-term
conventional_controls: Chelated iron granules or drench (EDDHA chelated iron most stable in alkaline soil)
prevention: Soil test before planting — know your pH
Amend soil pH to 5.5–6.5 for acid-loving plants
Plant acid-lovers away from concrete and lime-leaching materials
Use acidic mulches (pine bark, pine needles)
notes: Iron is plentiful in most soils but becomes unavailable to plants when pH is above 7.0. The fix is usually pH adjustment, not adding iron. Chelated iron spray is a fast fix but the underlying pH problem must be addressed for a permanent solution. Test soil pH every 2–3 years for acid-loving plants.

name: Mosaic Virus
latin: Tobacco Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, etc.
symptoms: Distinctive yellow and dark green mottled mosaic pattern on leaves — irregular patches of light and dark green or yellow creating a mosaic or mosaic-tile pattern. Leaves may be puckered, wrinkled, or distorted. New growth is stunted and malformed. Fruit may show color breaking, distortion, or internal browning. Plants grow slowly and produce poorly. Unlike nutrient deficiencies, mosaic virus causes an irregular pattern, not uniform yellowing.
where_to_look: Hold infected leaves up to light — the irregular mosaic pattern of light and dark is distinctive. Compare new and old growth. The pattern is most obvious on young leaves.

season.peak: Whenever aphid vectors are present
season.overwinters: In infected plant material and in certain weed hosts

life_cycle: Viruses are not organisms with life cycles — they are spread by aphid vectors (primarily), mechanical transmission (contaminated hands and tools), and in some cases through infected seeds. Aphids pick up the virus while feeding on infected plants and transmit it to healthy plants within minutes.
spreads_by: Aphid feeding (primary vector). Contaminated hands and tools. Infected seeds in some species. Tobacco products (TMV) — wash hands thoroughly after handling tobacco before touching plants.
organic_controls: NO CURE — remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Wash hands and tools with soap between plants
Remove weeds that serve as virus reservoirs
conventional_controls: No antiviral treatment exists for plants. Control aphid vectors.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties — most modern tomato varieties have TMV resistance (look for 'T' in resistance codes)
Control aphids rigorously
Do not smoke near plants or handle tobacco before touching plants
Wash hands between plants when working
Remove infected plants immediately to prevent spread
Destroy (do not compost) infected plant material
notes: There is no treatment for infected plants — removal is the only option. The good news: resistant varieties have made mosaic virus much less of a problem in modern gardens. The TMV resistance in tomatoes is so well established that most commercial varieties include it. Check seed packets for resistance codes: T=TMV, V=Verticillium, F=Fusarium, N=Nematode.

name: Early Blight
symptoms: Brown or dark spots on leaves with distinctive concentric rings — like a target or bullseye. Spots first appear on lower older leaves and work their way up the plant. A yellow halo surrounds the spots. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Stem lesions are dark, sunken, and may have concentric rings. Fruit lesions are leathery, dark, sunken, and form near the stem.
where_to_look: Lower leaves of tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, and eggplant. The target-ring pattern is the key identification feature.

season.peak: Warm humid weather — July and August
season.overwinters: In infected plant debris in soil

life_cycle: Fungal spores survive in plant debris and soil for years. Spread by water splash, wind, and insects. Warm temperatures (75–85°F) and high humidity accelerate spread. Infection requires wet leaves for 1–2 hours.
spreads_by: Rain splash from soil to lower leaves. Wind-dispersed spores. Contaminated tools.
organic_controls: Remove and dispose of affected leaves immediately
Copper fungicide spray — most effective organic
prevention: Mulch heavily to prevent spore splash from soil
Avoid overhead watering — water at base only
Morning watering so leaves dry before evening
Stake and cage plants for air circulation
2–3 year crop rotation
Remove and destroy all debris at end of season
notes: Early blight is the most common tomato disease in most of the US. Some defoliation of lower leaves is normal and acceptable. The key is to slow the progress upward — mulch, air circulation, and copper spray are the most important tools. Determinate tomato varieties often have better resistance than indeterminate types.

name: Late Blight
symptoms: Large irregular water-soaked gray-green patches on leaves that turn brown rapidly. White fuzzy mold visible on undersides of affected leaves in humid conditions. Stems show dark greasy-looking brown patches. Fruit has firm brown rot under the skin. The entire plant can collapse within a week in cool wet conditions. The same pathogen caused the Irish Potato Famine.
where_to_look: Leaf edges and tips first. Check undersides of affected leaves for the diagnostic white fuzzy sporulation in humid weather. Smell — late blight has a distinctive unpleasant potato-like odor.

season.peak: Cool wet weather — below 75°F with humidity above 90%
season.overwinters: In infected potato tubers left in ground. Cannot overwinter in frozen soil without a host.

life_cycle: Spreads at an extraordinary rate in cool humid conditions — new infection cycle every 5–7 days. Sporangia can travel miles on wind. Can devastate a planting in days.
spreads_by: Wind-dispersed sporangia travel miles. Rain splash. Infected transplants or potato seed pieces.
organic_controls: Copper fungicide — must be applied PREVENTIVELY before infection
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately (bag before moving)
biological_controls: No effective biological controls once infection is established
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (numerous are available)
Avoid overhead irrigation
Improve air circulation
Do not leave potato tubers in ground over winter
Scout regularly in cool wet weather
Apply copper spray preventively in high-risk conditions
notes: Late blight is one of the most destructive plant diseases. Once established in a planting, removal is often the only option to protect neighboring gardens. Report suspected late blight to your local extension service — it is important to track outbreaks. Never compost infected material — bag and discard or burn.

name: Botrytis (Gray Mold)
symptoms: Fuzzy gray mold covering affected tissue — the gray is the mass of fungal spores. Soft brown rot beneath the mold. Flowers turn brown and collapse. Stems develop gray moldy lesions and may collapse. Fruit rots from the stem end. Entire plants can collapse in cool wet weather. When disturbed, a cloud of gray spores is released.
where_to_look: Flowers, especially in wet conditions. Old or damaged plant tissue — Botrytis is a wound pathogen that enters through damaged or senescent tissue. Stems at soil level. Dense plantings with poor air flow.

season.peak: Cool humid conditions — spring and fall
season.overwinters: Sclerotia (hard resting bodies) persist in soil and plant debris for years

life_cycle: Botrytis infects through wounds and senescent tissue. Spores germinate in water on leaf surfaces. Cool temperatures (60–77°F) and high humidity are ideal. Infection can occur within hours of wet conditions. Produces billions of spores that easily spread by air.
spreads_by: Airborne spores — highly mobile. Spreads rapidly in humid, crowded growing conditions.
organic_controls: Remove dead and dying plant material promptly
prevention: Good air circulation — the most important prevention
Avoid overhead watering
Remove spent flowers and dying foliage promptly
Do not crowd plants
Morning watering so foliage dries before evening
Avoid wounds — Botrytis enters through wounds
notes: Botrytis is the same fungus that creates 'noble rot' in wine grapes — highly prized in Sauternes and other botrytized wines where the fungus concentrates sugars. In the garden, it is purely destructive. The key prevention is airflow — crowded plants in humid conditions are overwhelmingly most affected.

name: Deer
symptoms: Ragged torn damage on leaves and stems — deer have no upper front teeth so they tear rather than cut cleanly. Twigs are torn and shredded rather than cleanly severed (rabbits cut cleanly). Entire plants stripped of foliage overnight. Bark rubbed and stripped from young trees during antler rubbing season (fall). Hoof prints in soil. Damage height up to 6 feet (deer stand to reach).
where_to_look: Damage height — anything eaten from ground level to 6 feet is likely deer. Compare torn vs. clean cuts: deer tear, rabbits cut. Hoof prints confirm. Most active at dawn and dusk.

season.peak: Late summer through winter when natural forage is reduced
season.overwinters: Year-round pest

life_cycle: N/A — deer are a wildlife pest, not a pathogen.
spreads_by: Move through garden areas nightly. Home range of 1–3 square miles.
organic_controls: Physical fencing 8 feet tall (most reliable long-term solution)
Deer repellent sprays (putrescent egg solids most effective)
Irish Spring soap bars hung around garden perimeter
Human hair in mesh bags hung at deer nose height
conventional_controls: Commercial repellents containing putrescent egg solids (Liquid Fence, Plantskydd)
prevention: Plant deer-resistant species: lavender, rosemary, yarrow, foxglove, catmint, ornamental alliums (they avoid aromatic and toxic plants)
Fence young fruit trees individually
Repellents must be reapplied after rain
Vary repellent types — deer adapt to any single repellent over time
notes: The only reliable long-term solution is an 8-foot fence or a double fence (two 4-foot fences 3 feet apart — deer won't jump a barrier where they can't see a landing spot). Repellents require vigilance and rotation. Deer rapidly learn that a repellent is harmless and return. No plant is truly deer-proof when deer are hungry enough.

name: Root-Knot Nematodes
symptoms: Plants appear pale, stunted, and nutrient-deficient despite adequate fertilization. Yellowing. Wilting on hot days even with adequate soil moisture. The definitive diagnosis requires pulling a plant — roots show distinctive galls (rounded swellings) along their length. Galls range from small pea-sized to large irregular masses. Heavily infested roots cannot absorb water and nutrients effectively.
where_to_look: The only reliable diagnosis is examining the roots. Pull a struggling plant and look for rounded galls or swellings on the roots. Distinguished from normal root nodules (nitrogen-fixing bacteria on legumes) by their irregular shape and hard texture.

season.peak: Warm soil temperatures — above 65°F
season.overwinters: Survive in soil for years in egg masses

life_cycle: Microscopic roundworms that infect roots and cause the plant to form protective galls around them. Females lay hundreds of eggs inside root tissue. Multiple generations per year in warm soil. Cannot move more than a few inches through soil on their own.
spreads_by: Infested soil on tools, footwear, and transplants. Movement of infested soil. Water movement in heavy rain.
organic_controls: Solarize soil (clear plastic sheeting for 4–6 weeks in summer heat)
Marigolds as a cover crop — Tagetes patula specifically produces a nematicidal compound
Beneficial nematodes (Steinernema and Heterorhabditis species do not control root-knot)
Crop rotation with non-host plants (corn, grasses)
conventional_controls: No effective chemical nematicides widely available for home use
prevention: Do not move soil from infested areas
Clean tools thoroughly between plots
Plant resistant varieties — many tomato varieties are resistant (look for 'N' in resistance codes)
French marigolds (Tagetes patula) interplanted or as a cover crop — plant densely for 60+ days
Crop rotation with non-host plants
notes: Once established, root-knot nematodes are very difficult to eliminate. The most practical approach is management through resistant varieties, rotation, and marigold cover crops. Solarization is the most effective organic knockdown but requires 4–6 weeks of clear plastic in hot sunny weather. The 'N' resistance code on tomato seed packets indicates root-knot nematode resistance.

name: Fire Blight
symptoms: Shoot tips wilt and curl into a distinctive hook or 'shepherd's crook' shape and turn brown-black, as if scorched by fire — hence the name. Infected blossoms turn water-soaked then brown. The tissue death moves down the branch with a characteristic water-soaked margin between dead and live tissue. In humid weather a sticky amber-colored bacterial ooze drips from infected tissue. Entire branches or the whole tree can die rapidly.
where_to_look: Shoot tips curling into a hook shape — the most distinctive symptom. Blossoms failing to set fruit and browning. The transition zone between dead brown and live green tissue, often with a water-soaked margin.

season.peak: During bloom — spring
season.overwinters: In cankers on branches and the main trunk

life_cycle: Bacteria overwinter in cankers on infected wood. Ooze from cankers in spring is spread by bees, rain, and insects to open blossoms during pollination. Spreads rapidly in warm wet spring weather (65–85°F). Enters through blossoms, wounds, and succulent shoot tips.
spreads_by: Bees and other pollinators during bloom. Rain splash. Contaminated pruning tools (sterilize between cuts).
organic_controls: Prune out infected wood 12 inches below visible infection into healthy wood
Sterilize pruners in 10% bleach or 70% alcohol between every cut
Kaolin clay on blossoms during bloom
conventional_controls: Streptomycin spray during bloom (antibiotic — restricted use in many areas)
biological_controls: Bacillus subtilis (Serenade) spray during bloom — moderate effectiveness
prevention: Plant resistant varieties — essential in high-fire-blight areas
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer — lush growth is extremely susceptible
Prune in dry weather
Do not work in trees when wet
Sterilize tools
notes: Fire blight is one of the most serious tree fruit diseases. Tool sterilization between every cut is non-negotiable — the bacteria are easily spread on pruners. Burn or deeply bury pruned material. Resistant apple and pear varieties are the most practical long-term solution. Some heirloom apple varieties are extremely susceptible and should be avoided in fire-blight-prone areas.
